beats.caption: Four air bases. Seventy-two aircraft. One question every morning: what will fail next — and when?
Sahyadri, Aravalli, Himshikhar and Kaveri: monsoon, dust and heat, thin cold air, coastal salt.
Every engine replays a real NASA run-to-failure trajectory; seven more systems are simulated around it.
Spares move by road (cached OpenStreetMap routing) or by Vahak airlift.
Each ring is a base's readiness today: ready, watch, pulled from the line.
06:00Z — Himshikhar's data arrives. One aircraft moves to watch, and we can say exactly why.
The fleet readiness board: ready to deploy by type and base, with the readiness floor marked on every cell.
Himshikhar: 3,600 metres up. Every aircraft is a flight strip — health, limiting system, next action.
PR-S149, a Shikshak trainer. Eight systems, each with its own health — and hydraulics is the problem.
Hydraulics: pressure down about 20 psi, fluid 23 °C hot — effect sizes taken from a real hydraulic test rig.
